summary: Collects high-level requirements for tightly coupled SIP conferences, the kind where a central party manages the call. It examines a wide range of needs. Later documents are meant to map these onto existing protocol pieces and to define new extensions, together forming a guide for interoperable SIP conferencing applications.

subtitle: A list of what a SIP conference has to be able to do before anyone writes the protocol that does it.

tldr.problem: Before two implementations of SIP conferencing can talk to each other, someone has to say what a conference has to be able to do: how people join and leave, how the focus works, and what the rules of a conference are.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists requirements in nine groups, from finding a conference server through to side-bar conversations and instant messaging alongside a call, each marked as mandatory or optional.
tldr.outcome: Later documents are meant to map these requirements onto existing SIP primitives, define new extensions, and introduce new protocols where needed, giving a guide for building interoperable conferencing applications.

facts.label: Focus implementations
facts.value: A participant or a separate application server

today: RFC 4245 is an Informational memo published in November 2005, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It defines no protocol: it collects requirements that later documents are meant to map onto SIP primitives and extensions.

sections.title: Why This Requirements Document
sections.content:
This document examines a wide range of conferencing requirements for tightly coupled SIP conferencing. The requirements are grouped by subject so that work on the different areas can proceed in parallel.

Separate documents will map the requirements to existing protocol primitives, define new protocol extensions, and introduce new protocols where they are needed. Together, those documents are meant to provide a guide for building interoperable SIP conferencing applications. The memo defines no protocol itself; it says which of its requirements are mandatory, marked with the keyword MUST, and which are optional, marked SHOULD or MAY.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is a checklist for SIP conference software. It says what a conference has to be able to do, from finding the server that runs a call to deciding who may join and how people are told who is present.

sections.title: The Shape Of A Tightly Coupled Conference
sections.content:
A SIP conference is an association of SIP user agents, which are the participants, with a central point, the conference focus, which has direct peer-to-peer relationships with the participants by keeping a separate SIP dialog with each. The focus is itself a SIP user agent, with the ability to host conferences, including creating, maintaining and manipulating them using SIP call control and possibly other non-SIP means.

In this tightly coupled model the conference graph is always a star: the focus keeps the correlation between the conference's dialogs internally. The focus can be implemented by one of the participants, in which case it is typically capable of hosting only a simple ad hoc conference, established with SIP call control primitives alone. Or it can be a dedicated conference server, which offers richer functions such as simultaneous conferences, large scalable conferences, reserved conferences and managed conferences, and can support any subset of the advanced functions the document lists.

The media graph is a separate question from the signalling graph. It can be centralized, where the media sessions are established between the focus and each participant, or decentralized, where the media graph is a multicast or multi-unicast mesh among the participants, or any combination, and it can even differ per media type. Consequently the media processing, such as mixing, is done either by the focus alone or by the participants.

Two more sets of terms matter throughout. Conference policy means a set of parameters and rules, for example the maximum number of participants, whether a chair must supervise, whether the conference is password protected, how long it lasts, and how the media is mixed, set at the start of the conference and needing special privileges to change. Conference state means the information describing the conference in progress, including participants' information such as dialog identifiers, the media sessions in progress, the current loudest speaker and the current chair.
sections.plainLanguage: A conference is a star: a central focus keeps one SIP call with each participant and mixes what they send. The focus can be one of the participants or a dedicated server. The rules of the conference, such as its size and whether it needs a chair, are the conference policy.

sections.title: Joining, Leaving And Inviting
sections.content:
The discovery phase has to answer several questions: how to find the location of an arbitrary SIP conferencing server, how to tell from a SIP address of record whether that entity has focus capabilities, how to find the focus of a conference given its global identifier, and how to obtain the conference's properties and its state information given the same identifier. The requirements note that although some of this can be done by configuration or by proprietary conventions, there is consensus that standard means for implementing these functions by automata must be defined.

Creation needs a way to make an ad hoc conference identifier and a conference with given properties, and a way to make a reserved conference identifier for a conference with given properties. The properties may be set by default, by a profile, or explicitly.

Termination needs a way for a user agent, given a conference identifier, to disconnect all participants and terminate the conference, releasing the associated resources. A way may also be defined for asking a focus to turn a two-party conference back into a plain SIP point-to-point session and release the conferencing resources.

Participant manipulation has the most requirements of any group. A focus must be able to invite and disconnect a user agent that knows nothing but the basic SIP specification, and such a user agent must be able to dial in to a conference, in which case only the human knows they are connected. A focus must be able to invite another user agent to one of its conferences, and that invitation must establish a single SIP dialog between the two. Where there is already a dialog between two user agents and at least one of them has focus capability, the focus must be able to invite the other to one of its conferences without establishing an extra dialog. The invitation must carry a standard indication that it is a conference and the conference identifier.

On the way in, a user agent must be able to create an ad hoc conference with default properties and become a participant over a single SIP dialog, to activate a reserved conference and join it the same way, to dial in to an active conference it already knows the identifier of, and to join through the identifier of one of that conference's dialogs. A third party can be invited to a conference given its identifier or given the identifier of one of its dialogs, and a way should be defined for inviting a whole list of user agents at once.

Removal works in several directions: the focus must be able to remove a participant, a user agent must be able to remove a participant given the conference identifier or given the identifier of one of its dialogs, and a user agent must be able to remove all participants. A way may also be defined for removing a named subset of participants at once. On privacy, a focus should support a participant joining anonymously, so that their presence is announced but their identity is not, and joining in a hidden mode, where neither presence nor identity is disclosed. These imply that the anonymizing operations must be performed on the call control, the media control and the media content where appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Joining and leaving have to work for ordinary phones as well as conference-aware ones. A participant can dial in, be invited, or be pulled out, and a whole list can be invited or ejected at once. People can also join without their name being announced.

sections.title: Conference State And Focus Roles
sections.content:
Conference state is described as a virtual database describing the conference in progress, covering participants' information such as dialog identifiers and state, the media sessions in progress such as the contributing sources and encoding schemes, the current loudest speaker, and the current chair. It is the latest snapshot, triggered by changes in participants' state or in conference policy.

The state has to have a modular definition, so that different aspects can be accessed independently, and it must be possible to gather information about different aspects into a single report. A mechanism for extensible definition and registration of aspects that evolve over time must be present, and a default state report must be defined, holding at least a minimal useful set of information such as the list of current participants.

Changes have to be reported to interested parties, including people who are not in the conference, in a timely manner. A user agent must be able to say which state changes it is interested in, and what the minimum interval between reports should be. Recent changes must be able to be gathered into a single reporting event, and default change reports must be defined, holding at least the minimal useful information for participants, such as who joined and who left. On demand, any state information must be able to be disseminated to an interested party, which must also be able to ask for the state of a conference it names and say which subset of that state it wants and can receive.

Focus role migration covers what happens when the central point of the conference moves. A procedure must be defined for the current focus to delegate the role to another participant, for a participant to request that a focus transfer the role to it, and for an on-demand unconditional transfer to a different participant. A detection procedure for a focus failure condition must also be defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Participants need to know who is in the conference and who just joined or left. The memo also asks what happens if the machine running the conference dies or wants to hand the job to someone else in the call.

sections.title: Side-Bars, Cascading And Instant Messaging
sections.content:
A side-bar is a smaller conference inside the main one. A standard means must be defined so that a user agent who is not a participant can join or be invited to a side-bar, and so that a participant can create one with one or more other participants, join one, or be invited to one. A conference-unaware user agent must be able to create and take part in side-bar conferences, and this may be achieved by non-SIP means. A participant must also be able to create, join or be invited to any number of side-bars within the conference without establishing any additional SIP dialogs with the focus, and again this may be achieved by non-SIP means.

Cascading of conferences has different meanings in different contexts, and the document lists three. There is peer-to-peer chaining of signalling, where many ways exist to build the media graph. There are conferences with hierarchical signalling relations, again with many ways to build the media graph. And cascading may be used to distribute the media mixing only, with no requirement to distribute the signalling. Each of these leads to a different set of requirements.

Finally the memo asks that the SIMPLE presence and instant messaging architecture should fit into the general SIP conferencing architecture. Two scenarios must be addressed: one where a multimedia SIP conference and a multiparty instant messaging conversation take place among the same group of participants, and one where a side-bar, or a sub-instant-messaging conference, is held as part of a SIP conference.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside a conference, some participants may want to talk among themselves without the others hearing, and that has to work even for phones that know nothing about conferences. The memo also asks for conferences to fit together, and for a text chat to run alongside a voice conference.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Conferencing has some specific security requirements, and the memo summarizes them at a very high level. Every operation and function it describes has to be authorized by a focus or a participant, and conferences are expected to be governed by a set of authorization rules defined as part of the conference policy. For the conference policy to be implemented, the focus needs to be able to authenticate potential participants, and the normal SIP mechanisms, including Digest authentication and certificates, can be used for that. The conference-specific security requirements are to be discussed in detail in the protocol documents.

Conferencing also has privacy implications, some of which are discussed in the requirements themselves. The standard SIP mechanisms for a user agent to request privacy should be used by a focus, and they are to be detailed in the protocol documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Every action in a conference, such as inviting, removing or muting somebody, has to be allowed by the rules the conference was set up with. The focus checks who is joining using the usual SIP login methods.

viz.caption: WHAT A CONFERENCE HAS TO BE ABLE TO DO (RFC 4245 SECTION 3)

items.title: Discovery
items.text: Find a conferencing server, work out whether an address has focus capability, locate a conference by its identifier, and fetch its properties and state.

items.title: Creation
items.text: Create an ad hoc or a reserved conference identifier and set the properties, by default, by profile or explicitly.

items.title: Termination
items.text: Disconnect everyone and release the resources. A two-party conference may revert to a plain point-to-point call.

items.title: Joining and inviting
items.text: A plain SIP user agent can dial in or be invited, and both dial-in and dial-out use a single SIP dialog.

items.title: Removal and privacy
items.text: The focus can remove one participant or all of them, and a participant can join anonymously or hidden.

items.title: State and focus roles
items.text: A modular view of who is in the conference, change notifications, on-demand queries, and handing the focus role to someone else.

viz.caption: TWO WAYS TO BUILD THE MEDIA GRAPH (RFC 4245 SECTION 2)

left.title: Centralized media
left.desc: Media sessions are set up between the focus and each participant, and the focus does the mixing.

right.title: Distributed media
right.desc: The media graph is a multicast or multi-unicast mesh among the participants, and they do the mixing.
